title: Internal Dry Run #2 — Redwood Standard Demo v1 (Security persona Q&A)
summary: Internal dry run of the Standard Demo v1 with a security-first persona. Team rehearsed answers using the new Demo Tenant Security FAQ, focusing on: demo tenant isolation/sanitization, data retention and logging posture, encryption and key management, SSO/SAML/RBAC, audit logs/SIEM, data residency, and “do you train on our data.” Identified spots where talk track over-claims (SOC 2 language, retention defaults) and where we need crisp phrasing + slide/Console clickpath backups.
topics: Demo tenant isolation (hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC)
Encryption in transit/at rest; KMS/HSM phrasing
Audit logs, export, and SIEM integration language
What to show live vs what to state as capability
questions: What is the demo tenant’s actual retention window for request/response logs and metrics?
Can we say ‘no prompts stored’ or do we need to say ‘configurable retention’?
How do we answer ‘can we bring our own keys’ without getting dragged into implementation details?
What’s the approved language for SOC 2 (in progress vs certified) in a live demo?
Do we have a concrete audit log example we can show without exposing sensitive fields?
If a prospect asks for EU-only routing, what’s the exact supported story today?
next_steps: Soojin to tighten the security Q&A slide notes: approved language for retention, training on data, and SOC2 wording (align with Naomi/Marcus).
Markus to add a 60-second “security posture” preface and a 30-second “hosted vs dedicated vs private” fork cue in the talk track.
Naomi to confirm demo-tenant-specific defaults (retention window, logging toggles) and provide the exact safe phrasing for live demos.
Kevin to provide a sanitized audit log screenshot/example payload for the deck (no request bodies).
Sean to sanity-check that the demo dashboards reflect redaction/logging settings (no raw prompts in shared views).
action_items: Soojin Lee — Update speaker notes with approved security language (SOC2, retention, training on data) — Due 2024-08-19
Naomi Feldman — Validate demo tenant retention/logging defaults and write a 5-bullet ‘safe to say’ blurb — Due 2024-08-19
Kevin Osei — Create sanitized audit log example (screenshot + one JSON snippet) for the deck appendix — Due 2024-08-21
Markus Klein — Add security persona branching cues + ‘if asked’ answers to master script — Due 2024-08-20
Sean Gallagher — Confirm demo dashboards don’t surface request bodies; propose a quick pre-demo verification check — Due 2024-08-20
transcript:
Meeting Header
Title: Internal Dry Run #2 — Redwood Standard Demo v1 (Security persona Q&A)
Recorded: 2024-08-15 20:00 UTC
Duration: 47 min
Attendees: Markus Klein, Soojin Lee, Naomi Feldman, Talia Benson, Renee Sullivan, Nikhil Sharma, Marissa Cole, Sean Gallagher, Marcus Lin, Jordan Blake, Camila Reyes, Kevin Osei, Allison Grant

Auto-Summary (Fireflies)
- Focused on security objections and the Demo Tenant Security FAQ.
- Rehearsed how to answer retention, encryption, SSO/RBAC, audit logs, data residency.
- Flagged a few statements that need tighter, approved wording.

Topics
1) Security posture opener (how to frame in first 2 minutes)
2) Data handling: retention + logging + redaction
3) Encryption + key management language
4) Identity: SSO/SAML + RBAC
5) Audit logs + exports
6) Data residency and private deployment fork

Action Items (as discussed)
- Update talk track with “safe-to-say” phrases from FAQ
- Provide sanitized audit log example
- Confirm what’s actually enabled in demo tenant

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, we’re recording. This is dry run two for the standard demo, but we’re doing the security persona version. So, please interrupt. Naomi, Marcus, Kevin—like, stop us if we say anything squishy.

[00:17] Soojin Lee: Yep. I’ll run the narrative, Markus will drive in Console if needed. The goal is to make the Q and A feel crisp, not defensive, and not… overpromising.

[00:29] Talia Benson: And I’ll watch timing. We want the security sidebar to be, like, five-ish minutes unless they pull us deeper.

[00:39] Jordan Blake: Cool. Pretend I’m the CISO-ish buyer who’s already skeptical.

[00:44] Markus Klein: Great. Starting as if we just finished the “why Redwood” opener.

[00:52] Soojin Lee: Okay, so quick transition: “Before we go deeper on performance, I want to address security and deployment options upfront because it’s usually the gating item.”

[01:03] Soojin Lee: Redwood runs in three modes—hosted API, dedicated capacity, and private (VPC or on-prem). The control plane experience is consistent, so what we show in Console maps across those.

[01:17] Jordan Blake: I’m gonna jump in. Where is my data going? Are you storing prompts, are you training on it, what’s the retention. Like the classic three.

[01:27] Soojin Lee: Yep. So: we do not train foundation models on customer prompts by default. For retention, it’s configurable by deployment and tenant policy—

[01:37] Naomi Feldman: Pause, small tweak: say “we do not use customer inputs/outputs to train models” and then add “unless you explicitly opt in” if that exists. Otherwise just stop at “we don’t.”

[01:47] Soojin Lee: Got it. “We do not use customer inputs or outputs to train models.” Retention: logs and artifacts are configurable. In hosted, you can set retention policies and control what gets logged.

[02:01] Markus Klein: And for the demo tenant specifically, we run it sanitized: no customer data, only seeded sample prompts. Access is restricted to our field team, and the tenant has limited retention.

[02:13] Jordan Blake: What’s “limited.” Like seven days? Thirty? Never?

[02:18] Renee Sullivan: We should have the exact number, right?

[02:20] Naomi Feldman: For the dry run, don’t guess. Say: “we keep minimal operational logs for reliability and abuse prevention; exact retention is documented and can be configured contractually.” Then offer to follow up with the security FAQ.

[02:33] Soojin Lee: Okay. So: “We keep minimal operational logs needed for reliability and abuse prevention. The retention window is documented in our security FAQ and is configurable based on plan and deployment. For regulated workloads, private deployment gives you customer-controlled retention.”

[02:50] Jordan Blake: Does that mean you store request/response bodies?

[02:55] Markus Klein: By default, we focus on metadata—latency, token counts, error codes. For request and response bodies, we support redaction and logging controls. In private deployments, it can be fully within your environment.

[03:11] Marcus Lin: +1, but be careful: “by default” is slippery. We should say: “we can be configured to not store bodies; we recommend redaction; and we can show the exact settings.”

[03:21] Markus Klein: Yep. If it helps, in Console we can show the logging configuration page, but we probably don’t want to click too deep in a live demo.

[03:31] Soojin Lee: Right. We should have a one-slide “controls” view and then only click if asked.

[03:38] Camila Reyes: Also, no numbers on the slide. Keep it capability-focused.

[03:44] Soojin Lee: Okay. Next likely question: encryption. “Everything is encrypted in transit using TLS. At rest is encrypted, and we support key management integrations for enterprise deployments.”

[03:57] Jordan Blake: “Support key management” means what, bring my own key? HSM? Or you just have AWS KMS somewhere.

[04:05] Soojin Lee: The safe phrasing: “We integrate with customer-managed keys in private deployments, and for hosted/dedicated we use standard cloud KMS-backed encryption.”

[04:16] Kevin Osei: I’d add: don’t say HSM unless we mean it. Say KMS integration and, for HSM, “available depending on environment” or “via your cloud provider / your choice.”

[04:26] Soojin Lee: Good call. “KMS integration available; HSM is environment-dependent.”

[04:31] Jordan Blake: Identity. Can I do SAML, SCIM, granular roles.

[04:36] Markus Klein: For the Console and tenant access we support SSO and SAML for enterprise, RBAC roles, and audit logs for admin actions.

[04:45] Naomi Feldman: And emphasize least privilege: who can view prompts vs who can manage routes/keys.

[04:52] Markus Klein: Right. We have separate permissions for operational access. For the demo tenant, we keep roles very limited—SEs have run access, very few admins.

[05:02] Jordan Blake: Audit logs: show me. What events do you log.

[05:06] Markus Klein: In a live demo, I’d show the audit log page and filter for “policy change” events. But we need a sanitized screenshot too.

[05:16] Kevin Osei: I can produce a screenshot with fake user emails and no request bodies. It’ll show “route updated,” “RBAC role changed,” “API key created/rotated,” that kind of thing.

[05:28] Soojin Lee: Perfect. And we should state: audit logs can be exported to your SIEM.

[05:33] Allison Grant: Again, careful with “can.” If the integration is via webhook/export, say that. Don’t promise native Splunk integration unless it’s real.

[05:41] Soojin Lee: Okay: “We support audit log export (API/export) so customers can forward to their SIEM.”

[05:49] Jordan Blake: Data residency. If I’m EU telco, can you guarantee EU-only.

[05:54] Markus Klein: Today we can route traffic by region and pin to EU regions if you’re using our EU capacity. For strict residency and regulated constraints, we typically recommend Private in your VPC.

[06:08] Naomi Feldman: Add the line: “We won’t fail over across regions without policy.” That’s important.

[06:13] Markus Klein: Yes. Our routing policies are explicit. If you set EU-only, it won’t silently route to US as a fallback.

[06:22] Jordan Blake: Good. Now I’m going to do the annoying one: how do you isolate tenants in hosted.

[06:28] Soojin Lee: Multi-tenant hosted uses logical tenant isolation with strict access controls; dedicated provides isolation at the capacity level; and private gives you network isolation in your environment.

[06:41] Marcus Lin: That’s fine, but add “data plane isolation” and “per-tenant auth + quotas.” Also, don’t imply dedicated is the only “secure” option.

[06:50] Soojin Lee: Yep. “Hosted is secure by design; dedicated and private add stronger isolation controls for certain requirements.”

[06:58] Talia Benson: Timing check: we’re at seven minutes. Good, but keep the rest tighter.

[07:04] Markus Klein: I’m going to switch into the demo flow. Imagine we just addressed security posture. Now we show something that proves operational controls.

[07:12] Markus Klein: In Console, I’ll open the demo tenant’s Observability dashboard. This one breaks down latency, token counts, and error rates by route.

[07:21] Marissa Cole: Also mention: “no sensitive data in this tenant” before you show dashboards.

[07:25] Markus Klein: Good. “This tenant has only synthetic prompts and sample apps. No customer data.”

[07:33] Markus Klein: Okay, so you’ll see p50/p95 latency panels. And here’s a token-cost panel.

[07:43] Jordan Blake: I’m going to ask: are those dashboards showing request bodies.

[07:47] Markus Klein: No. These views are aggregated metrics. For deeper debugging, there is trace sampling, but it’s permissioned and can be configured to redact.

[07:57] Sean Gallagher: Add that in demo tenant, traces are limited. We don’t want someone clicking and seeing raw text.

[08:03] Markus Klein: Right. In demo tenant, we’ve locked down trace detail views.

[08:09] Jordan Blake: Okay, show me audit logs then. Not a dashboard.

[08:12] Markus Klein: We don’t have a good live clickpath here yet without risking weird data. We should use the sanitized screenshot Kevin mentioned, plus a short explanation.

[08:22] Soojin Lee: Agree. “In a customer tenant, audit logs capture admin actions like route changes, key rotation, RBAC changes; exportable via API.” Then show screenshot.

[08:33] Camila Reyes: That also keeps the demo from turning into a settings walkthrough.

[08:38] Markus Klein: Cool. Returning to the narrative: “We treat observability and governance as first-class.”

[08:46] Nikhil Sharma: Can we add the line about quotas/rate limits as a safety control? It’s security adjacent (abuse prevention).

[08:53] Markus Klein: Yes. “Per-tenant quotas, rate limiting, and usage analytics.”

[09:01] Jordan Blake: Rate limits are nice, but do you have DLP? Like prompt scanning.

[09:06] Soojin Lee: We should answer: “We provide validation hooks and integration points; many customers integrate their own DLP. For Private, you can integrate at your gateway.”

[09:18] Marcus Lin: Exactly. Don’t claim built-in DLP unless it exists. Say “policy hooks / middleware / gateway validation.”

[09:25] Markus Klein: And for demo tenant, we do input validation to prevent someone from pasting secrets.

[09:31] Naomi Feldman: That’s good. Also mention: “don’t paste real secrets in a demo.” Like, we can literally say it.

[09:38] Soojin Lee: Right. “We recommend using synthetic data in any live demo; Redwood’s demo tenant is configured that way.”

[09:46] Jordan Blake: Next one: incident response, SOC 2, ISO. What can we say.

[09:52] Naomi Feldman: Please do not freestyle. In demo: say “we can share our security package under NDA,” and “we have a mature security program.” If we are SOC 2 Type II, say it; if we’re in progress, say “in progress.” But don’t imply certified.

[10:07] Soojin Lee: Understood. “We have a security program aligned to common frameworks; security package available. Happy to provide the exact compliance posture in follow-up.”

[10:17] Jordan Blake: Okay. Now, show me something that proves you can keep systems reliable without seeing my data.

[10:24] Markus Klein: Great segue. We’ll show fallback routing. This is both reliability and control.

[10:31] Markus Klein: Here’s a route policy: primary model is pinned, and there’s a compatible fallback model variant if the primary hits an error budget or capacity issue.

[10:44] Jordan Blake: If it falls back, are you sending my data to a different vendor.

[10:48] Markus Klein: In Redwood’s platform, fallback stays within Redwood-managed capacity unless you configure external endpoints. And we can constrain fallback by region and by deployment mode.

[11:02] Naomi Feldman: Also say: fallback is opt-in and policy-based. “We don’t silently reroute without customer policy.”

[11:07] Markus Klein: Yep. “Explicit policy.”

[11:12] Soojin Lee: And if a security persona asks, the private/VPC story is: you can run the data plane in your network so requests never leave.

[11:22] Jordan Blake: Okay, private. Is it fully on-prem? Or just VPC.

[11:27] Markus Klein: We have private control plane options and on-prem packages for air-gapped or regulated environments. What’s most common is VPC.

[11:37] Marcus Lin: That’s fine, but keep it: “available; scoping required.” Don’t make it sound like we ship a Docker compose tomorrow.

[11:45] Markus Klein: Totally. “Private deployments are scoped with the platform team.”

[11:50] Talia Benson: We should practice the “when to pivot to Private” line. Soojin?

[11:55] Soojin Lee: “If you have strict data residency, custom retention requirements, or need your own keys and network controls, we typically move from hosted demo to a private architecture discussion.”

[12:09] Jordan Blake: That’s good.

[12:11] Markus Klein: Back to the demo: I’m going to run a sample request with streaming. Not super security-specific, but it proves low latency.

[12:21] Markus Klein: I’ll run the “support agent” prompt. Streaming response starts.

[12:27] Renee Sullivan: While it streams, insert the security line: “this is synthetic text.”

[12:31] Markus Klein: Yep. “This is synthetic.”

[12:34] (crosstalk)

[12:36] Markus Klein: You see tokens coming back. Now, the security question: are you logging this? In the demo tenant, we keep aggregated metrics only in shared views.

[12:48] Jordan Blake: But your engineers can see it.

[12:52] Marcus Lin: Answer should be: access is role-based and audited, and we support least-privilege. In private, your team controls access.

[13:01] Soojin Lee: “Access is permissioned and audited; and for sensitive workloads, private deployment keeps it in your environment.”

[13:09] Jordan Blake: Okay. Another: can you delete data on request.

[13:14] Naomi Feldman: Say: retention policies + deletion requests supported. But again, don’t give SLA unless it’s in the contract.

[13:22] Soojin Lee: “We support configured retention and deletion workflows; for private, you own the storage.”

[13:30] Markus Klein: Great. Now, I want to pivot to the FAQ itself. In a real call, we’d share the security FAQ PDF after the demo.

[13:38] Camila Reyes: Yep, and keep the live call clean. “We’ll send details.”

[13:42] Markus Klein: Okay, now let’s do a lightning round. Jordan, throw the top five security questions you expect.

[13:49] Jordan Blake: 1) Do you train on my prompts.

[13:52] Soojin Lee: “No, we do not use customer inputs/outputs to train models.”

[13:57] Jordan Blake: 2) Encryption.

[13:59] Markus Klein: “TLS in transit; encryption at rest; KMS-backed; customer-managed keys available in private deployments.”

[14:08] Jordan Blake: 3) SSO, RBAC.

[14:10] Soojin Lee: “Enterprise SSO/SAML; RBAC; least privilege; admin actions audited.”

[14:18] Jordan Blake: 4) Audit logs.

[14:20] Markus Klein: “Audit logs for admin actions; export via API/export for SIEM forwarding.”

[14:27] Jordan Blake: 5) Data residency.

[14:29] Soojin Lee: “Region routing and pinning; policy-controlled failover; for strict residency, Private in your VPC/on-prem.”

[14:38] Jordan Blake: Good.

[14:40] Sean Gallagher: Add one more: operational reliability without logging content.

[14:46] Markus Klein: Right. “We rely on metrics, token counts, error codes; content logging can be minimized or disabled depending on needs.”

[14:56] Naomi Feldman: Also, “we can do redaction.” That’s an important word.

[15:01] Markus Klein: Yep. “Redaction support.”

[15:04] Talia Benson: Okay, now we should practice a deeper drill-down question, because that’s where we get hand-wavy.

[15:10] Talia Benson: Example: “Tell me exactly what’s logged in hosted, where it’s stored, and who can access it.”

[15:17] Markus Klein: Good. I’d answer: “Operational metadata is logged for service reliability and billing—latency, token usage, request ids, error codes. Access to logs is restricted to authorized ops personnel; access is audited. For sensitive customers, we can configure reduced logging and/or recommend private deployment.”

[15:37] Marcus Lin: That’s pretty good. One more change: don’t say “billing” as a reason to store anything beyond usage counts. Say “usage metrics.”

[15:45] Markus Klein: Got it: “usage metrics.”

[15:48] Jordan Blake: I’m also going to ask: can you guarantee your support engineers can’t see prompts.

[15:55] Naomi Feldman: The honest answer is “we implement strict controls; for maximum assurance, private deployment ensures only your team has access.” Don’t promise “cannot” if technically they could under break-glass.

[16:08] Soojin Lee: So we say: “We follow least-privilege; access is audited; and for the highest assurance, private deployments keep data plane access within your org.”

[16:19] Markus Klein: Great.

[16:21] Marissa Cole: Also highlight: demo tenant is not a proxy for the most locked-down config. It’s a demo.

[16:27] Markus Klein: Yep.

[16:29] Camila Reyes: From a messaging standpoint, we should make sure the security answers don’t sound like “everything is Private.” Hosted is still credible.

[16:38] Soojin Lee: Agreed. “Hosted meets most needs; dedicated/private for incremental requirements.”

[16:45] Jordan Blake: Okay, what about pen tests.

[16:48] Naomi Feldman: “We can share summaries under NDA.” Not in a demo.

[16:52] Soojin Lee: “Available under NDA.”

[16:55] Markus Klein: Let’s shift to the deck flow. The security slide comes right before the routing/fallback slide.

[17:03] Markus Klein: So, we’d show: “Deployment options,” then “Security controls,” then “Reliability with fallback.”

[17:10] Renee Sullivan: The FAQ should be referenced as: “we have a security FAQ, and if you want, we can set up a dedicated security review.”

[17:19] Markus Klein: Good. “Dedicated security review” is a good CTA.

[17:23] Jordan Blake: One more trick: ask about data deletion and sub-processors.

[17:29] Soojin Lee: Sub-processors is tough in a live demo. We can say: “We maintain a list of sub-processors and share it with customers; for private deployments, customer controls the infra.”

[17:42] Marcus Lin: Yep, and don’t list vendors off the top of your head. Just say “documented list.”

[17:48] Soojin Lee: Got it.

[17:50] Markus Klein: Okay, I’m going to do a mini roleplay. Jordan, you’re a security lead, you stop us mid-demo.

[17:57] Jordan Blake: Alright. “Hey, before we continue, I need to know if you store prompts and responses. We can’t have PHI going into a system that stores it.”

[18:09] Soojin Lee: “Totally fair. Redwood supports configurable logging and retention. Many customers choose to minimize or disable content logging and rely on aggregated metrics. For PHI/regulated workloads, we typically recommend Redwood Private so the data plane runs in your VPC with your retention and key policies.”

[18:27] Jordan Blake: “So in hosted, you might store content.”

[18:31] Markus Klein: “Hosted can be configured based on your requirements, but if your policy is ‘no content leaves our network,’ then Private is the straightforward path.”

[18:43] Naomi Feldman: That’s good, but add: “We can scope it.” And avoid implying hosted always stores content.

[18:49] Markus Klein: Right. “We can scope the right configuration and document it.”

[18:55] Sean Gallagher: And we should have a standard line: “Don’t put PHI in the demo tenant.” Like, always.

[19:01] Renee Sullivan: Yes, put it in the pre-demo email + the checklist.

[19:05] Talia Benson: Okay, moving on: audit logs again, because prospects always ask.

[19:10] Kevin Osei: I’ll take that. The audit log events we should highlight are admin actions: route/policy edits, model version changes, key creation/rotation, SSO config, RBAC role assignments. We should avoid anything that looks like content logging.

[19:27] Soojin Lee: Good.

[19:29] Markus Klein: Another common Q: “Can we integrate with our IAM.” We can say SAML/SSO and SCIM if we have it.

[19:36] Marcus Lin: Do we have SCIM everywhere? If not, don’t say SCIM. Say “provisioning options available” or just stick to SAML + RBAC.

[19:44] Soojin Lee: Let’s stick to SAML + RBAC.

[19:47] Jordan Blake: And network: can I IP allowlist.

[19:50] Markus Klein: For hosted, we have network controls on enterprise tiers; for private, you control network policy fully.

[19:58] Naomi Feldman: Again: “available based on plan.” Fine.

[20:03] Markus Klein: Okay.

[20:04] (brief pause)

[20:06] Talia Benson: Can we address “who in Redwood can access what” with a simple model: break-glass, audited, least privilege.

[20:13] Marcus Lin: Yes. Standard: “Access is limited, reviewed, and audited; break-glass is controlled; and private deployments reduce Redwood access by design.”

[20:25] Soojin Lee: Perfect.

[20:27] Jordan Blake: Now I’ll ask about data egress. Are you calling out to third parties for safety or moderation.

[20:34] Markus Klein: Redwood’s inference is executed on our infrastructure (or yours in private). Optional add-ons like moderation are configurable, and we’d disclose any sub-processors. For the demo tenant, no third-party egress.

[20:49] Naomi Feldman: “No third-party egress” in demo tenant is good if true. But confirm.

[20:54] Markus Klein: Good point—let’s mark that as “to confirm.”

[20:58] Talia Benson: Action item: Naomi to confirm demo tenant egress posture.

[21:02] Naomi Feldman: Yep.

[21:04] Markus Klein: Okay, shift to the end-of-call CTA: “If security is a priority, we’ll schedule a security review and share our security FAQ and package under NDA.”

[21:15] Camila Reyes: That’s the right motion.

[21:17] Jordan Blake: Can we handle procurement-ish: DPAs, etc.

[21:21] Soojin Lee: “We have standard terms, DPAs available; our team will engage.” Not in demo.

[21:27] Markus Klein: Great.

[21:29] Sean Gallagher: I want to bring up a potential pitfall: dashboard screenshots. If we show an error panel with request examples, that could contain text.

[21:39] Markus Klein: Good catch. In demo tenant we should keep error analysis views sanitized.

[21:44] Allison Grant: We should prefer aggregated views in the deck.

[21:48] Markus Klein: Agreed.

[21:50] Marissa Cole: Also, in the Console clickpath, the “Traces” tab might expose content if someone has permissions. Make sure the role used for demos can’t open it.

[22:00] Markus Klein: We’ll confirm. Sean, can you check the role permissions.

[22:04] Sean Gallagher: Yes.

[22:06] Talia Benson: Okay, let’s do a quick run-through of the exact “safe phrases” we want everyone to memorize.

[22:13] Soojin Lee: 1) “We do not use customer inputs/outputs to train models.”

[22:18] Soojin Lee: 2) “Retention and logging are configurable; we can minimize content logging and rely on aggregated metrics; redaction supported.”

[22:28] Soojin Lee: 3) “TLS in transit; encryption at rest; KMS-backed; private supports customer-managed keys.”

[22:37] Soojin Lee: 4) “SSO/SAML and RBAC; access is least-privilege and audited.”

[22:44] Soojin Lee: 5) “Audit logs for admin actions; export available for SIEM workflows.”

[22:51] Soojin Lee: 6) “Data residency supported via region pinning and explicit routing policy; no silent cross-region failover.”

[23:00] Jordan Blake: Good. Add: “We can share security package under NDA.”

[23:04] Soojin Lee: 7) “Security package under NDA.”

[23:08] Markus Klein: Nice.

[23:10] Renee Sullivan: For enablement, we should put these as a one-pager.

[23:14] Talia Benson: Yep.

[23:16] Markus Klein: Any other red flags?

[23:18] Marcus Lin: Just one: don’t say “SOC2” casually. Say “we can share our current compliance posture.” If we’re certified, fine, but don’t imply.

[23:28] Soojin Lee: Understood.

[23:30] Kevin Osei: And on audit logs: emphasize it’s admin actions, not content.

[23:35] Markus Klein: Great.

[23:37] Camila Reyes: Also, if asked “who are your subprocessors,” don’t list. Say “documented list, provided during security review.”

[23:45] Soojin Lee: Got it.

[23:47] Markus Klein: We’ve got ~20 minutes left. Let’s practice a rough segment where we get pulled into security, then we pull back to demo value.

[23:56] Markus Klein: Soojin, start from “routing and fallback.” Jordan, interrupt with a security question.

[24:03] Soojin Lee: “Here, we’re showing our routing policy. You can define a primary model and a fallback variant to keep your app online—”

[24:12] Jordan Blake: “If you fall back, are you changing model behavior and exposing us to risk. Also, where is that request processed.”

[24:21] Soojin Lee: “Great question. Fallback is explicit and policy-controlled. You can constrain it by region and deployment. In private deployments, both primary and fallback run within your environment. And in any mode, we recommend pinning model versions and running evals so behavior changes are controlled.”

[24:41] Marissa Cole: Nice—mention evals, that’s strong.

[24:44] Markus Klein: Great. Then we pull back: “Operationally, you can observe when fallback happens and why.”

[24:51] Soojin Lee: “And you can see it in Console—events, error rates, and performance.”

[24:57] Jordan Blake: “Do you log the content when fallback triggers.”

[25:01] Markus Klein: “No, fallback events are metadata. Content logging is controlled separately.”

[25:08] Naomi Feldman: Good.

[25:10] Sean Gallagher: Another common one: “Do you support customer-provided certificates / mTLS.” We should have a stance.

[25:17] Marcus Lin: If we don’t support mTLS broadly, say “available in private deployments / scoped.” Don’t claim default.

[25:24] Soojin Lee: Okay.

[25:26] Talia Benson: We should capture these “not default, scoped” items.

[25:31] Markus Klein: I’ll note: mTLS = scoped.

[25:34] Jordan Blake: What about vulnerability management / SAST/DAST. Prospects ask.

[25:40] Naomi Feldman: “Security program; share docs.” Don’t go into toolchain.

[25:44] Markus Klein: Right.
